Dissolution of the Monasteries
dis-uh-LOO-shun
n. (the suppression of all religious houses in England, Wales and Ireland between 1536 and 1541, and the transfer of their lands to the crown)
From Latin dissolutio, a loosing apart, from dissolvere, to unbind; the technical term in the surrender deeds.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Between 1536 and 1541 every religious house in England, Wales and Ireland was suppressed: about eight hundred communities, some ten thousand religious, and property worth perhaps a fifth of the kingdom's landed wealth. The lesser houses went by statute in 1536, the greater by surrender and attainder thereafter, and the lands were sold within a generation to a gentry who would never permit their return. A Reformed dictionary must say two things at once and resist the temptation to say only one. The doctrinal case against the houses was substantially sound: masses for the dead, relic shrines, purchased merit. The confidence of their defenders was also the confidence Jeremiah demolished: “Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these” (Jer 7:4). And our Lord's word over a greater building settles what buildings are worth: “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines dissolution as the act of liberating or breaking up, the separation of the parts of a body; and suppression as the act of putting down, destroying or concealing.

expand to see more

DISSOLUTION, n. The act of liberating or breaking up. The separation of the parts of a body which destroys its form.

SUPPRESSION, n. The act of suppressing, crushing or destroying. The act of concealing; a keeping secret.

SURRENDER, n. The act of yielding or resigning one's person or the possession of something into the power of another.

ATTAINDER, n. Literally a staining, corruption or rendering impure; a corruption of blood. The judgment of death, or sentence of a competent tribunal upon a person convicted of treason or felony.

SACRILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things, or of alienating to common purposes what has been consecrated to religious uses.

Key Scripture

Jer 7:4 — "Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these."

Mat 24:2 — "And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down."

Jer 7:11 — "Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, even I have seen it, saith the LORD."

Mic 2:2 — "And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage."

Modern Corruption

Eight hundred houses suppressed in five years, a sound doctrinal case, and a transfer of a fifth of England to courtiers.

expand to see more

The corruption is on both sides of the account, and the Protestant half must be stated plainly. Jeremiah's charge against the temple establishment applies to the houses: “Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?” (Jer 7:11). But the men who dissolved them were not reformers acting on a doctrine of the church; they were a king who needed money and courtiers who wanted land, and Micah's description fits them exactly — “they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away” (Mic 2:2).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a right judgement may be executed by the wrong hands for the wrong reasons, and that God is not thereby implicated in the motives. Nothing in Scripture suggests that the removal of an idolatrous institution sanctifies the men who profited; Assyria was the rod of God's anger and was judged for the swing. “See ye not all these things?” (Mat 24:2) was said about a temple God himself had commanded.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin dissolvere, to unbind; Hebrew sheqer (H8267), falsehood; Hebrew meharah, a den; Greek kataluo (G2647), to throw down; Hebrew gazal (H1497), to seize.

expand to see more

Latin dissolutio — a loosing apart; the word in the surrender deeds.

Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; “Trust ye not in lying words” (Jer 7:4).

Hebrew parits (H6530) — a robber, a violent one; “become a den of robbers in your eyes” (Jer 7:11).

Greek kataluo (G2647) — to loosen down, to destroy; “that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2).

Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to take by force; “and take them by violence” (Mic 2:2).

Usage

"“The temple of the LORD, are these” (Jer 7:4) — the defenders' confidence, demolished."

"“a den of robbers” (Jer 7:11) — the charge against the houses."

"“and houses, and take them away” (Mic 2:2) — the charge against the dissolvers."
